desc: Derive the precise effect of operations A and B on the run-length encoding of the string, including boundary creation/deletion, and identify the exact invariant (e.g., positions of run boundaries modulo X+Y, total ones).

Write and run a brute-force BFS over all binary strings for small N (≤ 12) with several (X, Y) pairs to compute exact equivalence classes, then test the conjectured invariant: same reduced run sequence (1-run lengths mod Y, 0-gap lengths mod X, with 0-residue runs/gaps deletable) plus per-residue-class counts mod gcd(X,Y); report whether the conjecture holds or a counterexample. (Result: conjecture REFUTED — e.g. N=4, X=2, Y=1: "0110" vs "1001" share signature but differ; frozen states and gap-vs-X geometry matter.)

Run the confluence harness (code in CURRENT SOLUTION) for all N ≤ 12, X+Y ≤ N, and record which of the three canonical-form variants (A-leftmost fixpoint, B-leftmost fixpoint, no-A-move fixpoint) is class-consistent against the exact BFS equivalence classes; capture the first failing class details and the frozen-fixpoint diagnostics for each variant. (Result: all three variants class-consistent on all 275 parameter sets; #distinct A-fixpoints == #equivalence classes in all diagnostics.)

Prove or gather more evidence for confluence of the A-leftmost reduction: (a) local confluence check — for all small strings, verify that any two one-step reductions can be joined (Newman's lemma + termination ⇒ global confluence); (b) randomized order-independence tests for larger N (N up to ~10^4) comparing leftmost-A fixpoint vs random-order A-reduction fixpoint.

Design an efficient O(N) (or O(N log N)) algorithm to compute the no-A-move normal form: likely a left-to-right stack simulation that maintains the reduced string and only re-checks a window of length X+Y around the top of the stack after each push; verify it matches the naive fixpoint on all small cases and random large cases.
Implement the final solution: parse stdin, handle edge cases (S == T, count mismatch → No, X+Y > N → only S==T is Yes, X=Y, Y>X), compute canonical form for S and T, print Yes/No.
Validate the implementation against the brute-force BFS checker on random small cases (varying N, X, Y) to confirm correctness before finalizing.
